The card gives the component sizes 5 and 2 and the largest, 5." width="100%"} Returns the number of nodes in the biggest connected piece of the graph, often called the *giant component*. For undirected graphs this is the largest connected component. For directed graphs it is the largest *weakly* connected component: edge direction is ignored, so two nodes count as connected if there is any path between them when every edge is treated as two-way. The size of the giant component is the standard way to measure how well a network holds together, which makes it useful for: - tracking fragmentation in robustness studies, after `node_percolation()` or `edge_percolation()` - checking at a glance whether a graph is connected (the result equals the node count) - normalizing other statistics by the size of the main component The computation is a breadth-first traversal that touches every node and edge once. Isolated nodes form components of size `1`, and an empty graph returns `0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes in the largest connected component (weakly connected for directed graphs), or `0` for an empty graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} This graph has two pieces: a chain of four nodes and a separate pair. The largest component therefore has four nodes, even though the graph has six in total: ::: {#46939f58 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("E", "F")]) ) (graph.count_nodes(), graph.largest_component_size()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6, 4) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, edge direction does not matter. Here B and C both point into A and nothing points out of A, yet all three nodes still form one weakly connected component: ::: {#6ed4c0b6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("B", "A"), ("C", "A")]) ) directed.largest_component_size() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A common robustness check compares the giant component before and after random failures. A 20-node ring is a single component, but removing a quarter of its nodes at random cuts it into separate arcs, the longest of which has only 8 nodes: ::: {#937fc6f2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ring = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(20) damaged = ring.node_percolation(q=0.25, seed=1) (ring.largest_component_size(), damaged.largest_component_size()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (20, 8) ``` ::: :::
